510.bp: When networks like financial transactions or social graphs start exhibiting weird activity—fraudulent rings, unusual behavior—you want to catch it before it causes real harm. The challenge is that these networks have far more normal activity than anomalies, so any detection system needs to learn what 'normal' looks like from very few labeled examples.
510.wh: Most unsupervised learning methods randomly alter the network structure to teach patterns, but cutting edges or adding noise wipes away the very clues that tell you something is anomalous. At the same time, comparing a node to other random negatives teaches almost nothing, since most random pairs are obviously different. The real bottleneck is that you need both meaningful positive examples (things like the anomaly) and hard negatives (things close to the anomaly but normal).
510.ap: This work uses 'counterfactual' reasoning—imagining what the network would look like if you changed specific aspects—to build smarter training pairs. Instead of random edits, it identifies which nodes are structurally complex and worth studying, then carefully constructs synthetic variations that keep the anomalous character intact. For hard negatives, it generates believable normal versions. But doing this for every node is expensive, so the method picks a strategic subset to analyze deeply, cutting computational cost by roughly two-thirds.
510.ww: The insight is that anomalies live in the 'hard to explain' parts of the network—places where the structure and node properties don't play nicely together. By targeting these places and asking 'what if we changed this one property,' you teach the model what really makes something anomalous, rather than just teaching it to memorize outliers. The hard negatives then force it to distinguish real anomalies from normal variations.
510.po: On real-world financial graphs and other networks, this method catches anomalies as well or better than existing approaches, while using a third less computation. It's particularly strong when anomalies hide in complex structure-attribute interactions—the kind of subtle fraud or manipulation that simple statistical methods miss.

511.bp: Nearest-neighbor search powers everything from web search to question-answering systems that pull in outside knowledge: you ask a question, the system finds the thousand most similar documents or vectors, then uses those to answer you. The challenge is that both the data and what people ask for changes over time—old query patterns stop being relevant, new documents arrive, and the system can't afford to rebuild from scratch constantly.
511.wh: Current systems use static graphs that connect each point to its nearest neighbors, which works fine at the start but degrades over months. When you try to fix this by pruning edges and adjusting connections, you face three problems at once: the data distribution itself shifts (drift), different parts of the graph age differently (some clusters get many new neighbors, others don't), and testing whether a change helps requires running expensive queries on the whole graph.
511.ap: The method treats graph pruning as a decision problem solved by bandits—a framework from statistics for picking actions when you don't know the full outcome. It learns which pruning strategies work best for different regions of the graph by testing them on small batches, then adapting as patterns drift. It uses metadata (what kind of region is this) to customize decisions per region, and it batches feedback so you don't have to evaluate the whole graph every time.
511.ww: Bandits excel at learning under uncertainty when feedback is partial and costly. By separating out temporal drift detection (noticing when patterns shift) from spatial adaptation (finding region-specific tweaks), the method avoids throwing away all prior knowledge when conditions change. Batching feedback reduces the cost of each evaluation, so you can adapt frequently without exhausting compute budgets.
511.po: In real systems with thousands of documents and shifting query traffic, this keeps search accuracy and speed stable for months without expensive reindexing. The mathematical guarantee ensures that over time, you're provably not losing too much quality while adapting to drift.

512.bp: Predicting how many people will move through subway stations helps cities manage congestion, plan crowding relief, and route buses efficiently. The challenge is multimodal: you need video feeds (crowds, density), sensor data (gate entries), weather, and schedules—but each station owner keeps their data private, creating isolated silos across a city.
512.wh: Combining multimodal data is hard because the signals are in different 'languages'—video sees physical presence, transaction logs count paid entries, and some of these contradict each other. Existing models struggle to align these signals. Also, capturing patterns over hours and days requires models that can 'remember' far-back history, which traditional approaches do poorly. Finally, privacy regulations forbid centralizing station data, so you can't naively train one global model.
512.ap: This work builds a federated system where each station trains its own model while a central server coordinates without seeing raw data. Within each local model, a 'cross-modal alignment' module learns to translate between video and transaction signals—essentially teaching them to agree on ground truth. The prediction engine uses two parallel pathways: one that's very efficient at short-range memory (Mamba), another that sees all history at once (Transformer), both running side-by-side. A blockchain-based reputation layer tracks which stations are trustworthy and personalizes how much each contributes.
512.ww: Mamba and Transformers have opposite trade-offs: Mamba is fast but can't see everything at once, while Transformers see everything but are slow. Running them together and merging predictions lets you catch both local patterns and global trends. The cross-modal alignment works because both video and transactions are observing the same underlying phenomenon—you just need to learn the translation. Federated learning keeps data private while still building a coordinated model.
512.po: Predictions of subway crowding improve over centralized models, even with data staying at each station. The system scales to multiple cities (tested in Hangzhou and Shanghai) and adapts as usage patterns shift, without exposing sensitive commuting data.

513.bp: Knowledge graphs—enormous databases that encode facts like 'Einstein worked at Princeton'—power intelligent assistants and search engines. But real-world graphs are always growing: new entities appear, new relationships are discovered. The system needs to continuously absorb these updates and keep its internal representations (which encode 'who is Einstein' and 'what does worked-at mean') up-to-date and accurate.
513.wh: Learning embeddings (compact mathematical summaries of each entity and relation) is computationally expensive. When the graph grows, naively retraining on everything wastes resources; selectively updating some embeddings while leaving others frozen causes forgotten knowledge to resurface or new entities to have weak representations. The core issue is deciding which parts of the graph matter most—degree (how connected something is) is a crude signal that misses subtle structural importance.
513.ap: This method introduces two key ideas: first, it identifies which new entities matter most by looking not just at how many connections they have, but how topologically central or novel they are within the evolving structure. These entities get allocated more of the model's representational capacity. Second, rather than using a fixed training objective, it dynamically adjusts the 'target' based on what the model is trying to predict—if it's learning a one-to-many relationship (one boss, many employees), it sets a looser target than for one-to-one relationships.
513.ww: Topological importance correlates with real-world impact better than simple degree counts—think of a new regulatory agency (low degree but structurally pivotal) versus a minor contact. By adapting the training target to the type of relationship, you prevent the model from forcing mismatched constraints. If a relationship is inherently 'fuzzy' (many possible answers), making the model choose one 'correct' answer teaches it badly.
513.po: The system updates knowledge graphs faster than existing methods while maintaining or improving accuracy in downstream tasks like question-answering. It scales to large graphs that evolve continually, making it practical for real-world deployments where facts change daily.

514.bp: Asking a camera to identify and track objects—'find all cars, and follow this pedestrian across frames'—is foundational to autonomous systems, surveillance, robotics, and video analysis. The field has been accelerating with new deep learning models, but there's no single clear picture of where it's heading or what problems remain.
514.wh: Object detection (finding bounding boxes) and tracking (linking the same object across frames) were historically isolated problems with separate models and datasets. Newer models blur these boundaries, and language is entering the picture: 'find vehicles that are red and moving left.' Yet surveys fall out of date quickly, standards are fragmented (different benchmarks measure different things), and emerging combinations like 3D-with-language or diffusion-based tracking aren't well understood.
514.ap: This is a comprehensive review examining over a hundred papers across many variants: 2D detection, 3D with multiple camera views, fusion of visual and language information, and generative approaches using diffusion models. It catalogs which datasets and metrics dominate, how often each pairing of tasks appears, and what problems researchers keep hitting. It then surfaces patterns: models converging toward unified frameworks, generative models enabling temporal reasoning, and uncertainty quantification becoming more central.
514.ww: Broad surveys work by clustering similar approaches, analyzing what assumptions underlie each cluster, and identifying gaps or overlaps. By tracking which datasets and metrics are used over time, you see which problems matter to practitioners and which get overlooked. Cross-task patterns emerge naturally when you look across silos—the convergence of detection and tracking, for instance, becomes obvious when you see the same architectural principles solving both.
514.po: Researchers gain a map of the field: which combinations work well together (multimodal + diffusion), where data is scarce (open-world tracking), and which emerging capabilities (language-grounded tracking, 3D uncertainty) merit focus. Practitioners evaluating a detection system can benchmark against unified standards rather than fragmented metrics.

515.bp: Companies deploy machine learning models to handle countless decisions: approving loans, moderating content, recommending products, predicting failures. But data in the wild is messy—it has biases, noise, and gradual shifts (last year's buying patterns don't predict this year's). A bad model makes bad decisions at scale, causing real harm. Before deploying, you need to know: how stable is this model when conditions change?
515.wh: Model robustness is hard to measure. Standard accuracy (what percentage of predictions are correct) doesn't tell you about fairness (does the model treat everyone equally) or stability (does it work on new data). Testing by hand is expensive and incomplete. Causal reasoning—understanding why a model makes decisions—can quantify robustness, but it requires specialized technical knowledge that most practitioners don't have.
515.ap: This tool automates robustness assessment using causal methods. You upload your data or pick from supported domains (loan approval, sentiment, recommendations, forecasting), specify protected groups or fairness constraints, and the tool computes metrics measuring how predictions shift when you perturb the data or change sensitive attributes. It visualizes trade-offs: if you gain fairness, how much accuracy do you lose? You can test multiple candidate models side-by-side on a level playing field.
515.ww: Causal reasoning quantifies 'how much does this change affect outcomes' in a way that raw statistics don't. By asking 'if we changed this person's age, how would the decision flip,' you get a precise fairness metric. Trade-off visualizations work because they're grounded in real numbers—you're not asking people to judge fairness abstractly, you're showing them: this model is 94% accurate but 12% less accurate for protected group X.
515.po: Developers can confidently select models for deployment, knowing concrete numbers about robustness, fairness, and stability. The tool is model-agnostic (works with any trained model) and task-independent, so it applies to loan decisions, hiring systems, or video classification. Decision-makers get evidence-based guidance rather than hunches.

516.bp: Recommendation systems that suggest movies or products to users work best with lots of user history, but new users have none—they get generic suggestions that don't match their taste. The trick is to transfer knowledge from related domains: if you know what this person watched on Netflix, can you infer what they'll buy on Amazon? This cross-domain transfer solves the cold-start problem.
516.wh: Most cross-domain recommendation ignores a key signal: items are often similar across domains (thriller films and thriller novels), but existing methods only look at user-item interactions. When models teach the system to blur all domains together with Gaussian noise (like diffusion models do), they wash away personalized preferences—the new user ends up indistinguishable from everyone else. The challenge is transferring the essence of what a user likes while respecting that tastes differ between domains.
516.ap: Instead of adding noise (the diffusion model approach), this method uses a smooth-then-sharpen process. It starts by blurring user preferences and item similarities in a gentle, structured way using heat diffusion (a continuous mathematical process, not random noise), which preserves the item-item relationships across domains. Then it iteratively sharpens and recovers the preferences specific to the cold-start user. All of this is cast as solving a differential equation (ODEs), a principled mathematical framework.
516.ww: Heat diffusion is reversible and structure-preserving; adding Gaussian noise is not. By modeling the process mathematically (via differential equations), the system can reverse the smoothing precisely. Keeping item-item similarities intact means that if the user liked spy thrillers, the system learns that spy thrillers in the target domain should matter. The sharpening process recovers preferences iteratively, letting you see what's recovered at each step and adjust if needed.
516.po: Cold-start users get personalized recommendations informed by other domains, matching quality of recommendations for established users. The ODE-based approach outperforms diffusion-based methods because it preserves nuance and doesn't destroy personalization with irreversible noise.

517.bp: People expressing suicidal thoughts online leave traces in their social media posts and the reactions they get. Detecting and intervening early can save lives. The challenge is that most online signals are noise—people express dark thoughts but don't act. You need to learn which patterns in posts and comments actually predict risk versus those that are just venting.
517.wh: Most existing methods treat all comments as noise or a single aggregate signal: 'did others reply supportively or not.' But comments are heterogeneous—supportive feedback from close friends has different psychological weight than criticism from strangers, and its protective effect changes over time. Traditional temporal models learn 'this person's communication style,' but that overfits; a different person with a similar style may have different underlying risk. The real problem is untangling what about the trajectory matters from what's just individual habit.
517.ap: The method separates comments into two types: supportive (protective factors) and harmful (risk factors), and aligns them with clinical understanding of suicide risk. It then uses an adversarial learning technique—one model predicts next-month risk while another tries to guess whether a given time period belongs to this user or a different user—to force the system to learn general patterns rather than 'this person is always sad.' This disentanglement allows the model to transfer learning to new users.
517.ww: Supportive and harmful comments work through different psychological mechanisms; treating them the same loses signal. Adversarial disentanglement works because if a model is learning person-specific quirks (Alice is always sad on Tuesdays), the adversary can easily guess 'that's Alice.' But if it's learning genuine risk dynamics, the adversary can't tell users apart, forcing the model to generalize. This improves transfer to new users you've never seen.
517.po: The system predicts suicide risk better than methods using only posts or generic comment signals, particularly on new users where overfitting to individual style would be most damaging. It provides interpretable separation: here's how supportive feedback helped, here's how harmful comment clusters hurt.

518.bp: Models trained on sensitive data—medical records, financial histories, personal information—can be hacked or subpoenaed, exposing private details. Laws like GDPR and CCPA demand the right to be forgotten: if someone asks to delete their data from the system, the model should be retrained as if that person never existed. But retraining from scratch is impractically expensive at scale.
518.wh: Machine unlearning—erasing the influence of specific data without full retraining—is hard because neural networks compress data into dense parameter vectors; you can't simply 'undo' an influence. Naive approaches that try to downweight certain samples are unstable: the model becomes fragile, and other users' information can leak. You need both strong privacy guarantees and a model that still works well after forgetting.
518.ap: This method combines pruning and unlearning. First, it sparsifies the model by removing less-important connections, which also breaks the tight coupling between model parameters and training data—loosely speaking, the model becomes less dependent on memorizing specifics. Then, it uses gradient-based projection to actively remove dependencies on the data to be forgotten, while protecting remaining data. It applies different levels of pruning per network layer to prevent 'layer collapse' where some layers become useless.
518.ww: Sparsity and privacy are related: a dense network that's forced to remember many details is more vulnerable, while a sparse network relies on broad patterns. Gradient projection is targeted: instead of just downweighting a sample, you identify the exact directions in parameter space that encode its influence and push parameters away from those directions. Layer-wise pruning prevents any single layer from carrying all the unlearning load, which could break it.
518.po: After unlearning specific users' data, the model remains accurate, private (resists attacks trying to recover deleted data), and stable (future training doesn't erode earlier unlearning). Compared to full retraining, it's roughly 65% faster, making privacy compliance practical for large models.

519.bp: Recommendations improve when you combine data from multiple sources—music taste plus viewing history plus purchase behavior all inform what you might enjoy. But domains have gaps: you may be a voracious reader but sparse in ratings. The usual trick is to pool data across domains, but if movie taste and book taste are different, naive mixing hurts predictions.
519.wh: Models built to merge domains often use complex fusion architectures that learn separate representations per domain then combine them, requiring lots of compute and engineering. But the core problem isn't model capacity; it's that raw multi-domain data has 'domain gap'—the patterns differ subtly. You can't just concatenate or mix sequences from different domains; the model overfits to dataset-specific noise rather than learning generalizable patterns.
519.ap: Instead of redesigning models, this work regenerates the target-domain data to be richer and more coherent. It uses contrastive decoding (a technique that compares alternatives and picks the best) to adaptively weave in context from source domains into target-domain sequences. Basically, it asks: for this user's movie history, what would their book history plausibly be? Then it synthesizes more realistic, augmented sequences that standard models can learn from cleanly. The framework is data-centric, not model-centric.
519.ww: Data-centric approaches work when the real bottleneck is data quality, not model architecture. By synthesizing enriched sequences that respect domain-specific patterns (books have different temporal dynamics than movies), the model learns alignable structure. Standard simple models trained on good synthesized data often outperform fancy models on mixed data because they're not fighting noisy contradictions.
519.po: Recommendation accuracy improves, and the gains transfer to various backbone models—you're not locked into one specific architecture. By avoiding complex fusion modules, the framework is simpler to implement and faster to train. Code is released, enabling adoption.

520.bp: Deepfake videos—synthetic face swaps that look photo-realistic—can spread misinformation, defame people, and undermine trust in video as evidence. Detectors need to distinguish real from AI-generated faces reliably, even when the synthetic face is extremely convincing.
520.wh: Deepfakes made with modern tools are nearly pixel-perfect to the eye; simple checks like 'look for compression artifacts' fail. The synthesis process is imperfect though—tiny inconsistencies in muscle coordination (action units—the anatomical basis of facial expressions), temporal coherence, and holistic context leak out. The problem is that these signals are subtle, scattered across frames, and easy to confuse with normal video noise or poor lighting.
520.ap: This method combines two analysis pathways. One extracts action units—the fundamental muscle coordinates underlying expressions—and tracks how they coordinate over time. The other learns high-level semantic context using adaptive attention, essentially asking 'does this face and background cohere given the expressed emotion.' Both pathways feed into a unified model that learns to flag synthesis-induced inconsistencies invisible to either channel alone.
520.ww: Physiological signals (muscle movements) and semantic consistency (expression matches context) are orthogonal: you can have coherent expression without correct muscle coordination, or vice versa. By checking both, you catch more forgeries. Adaptive attention lets the model focus on regions or frames where inconsistencies are most likely, rather than treating all frames equally. The combination reveals what no single modality captures.
520.po: The detector achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on deepfake benchmarks and generalizes well to videos made with new tools or methods not seen during training. It's particularly effective on high-quality commercial deepfakes—the kind that matter most for misinformation.

521.bp: Graph neural networks—models that learn from networks of connected data—are powerful but overfit: they memorize training examples rather than learning generalizable patterns. Data augmentation (adding random variations to training data) is a proven way to reduce overfitting, but existing graph augmentation is coarse: you might randomly delete edges or mix node features, losing important structure.
521.wh: The bottleneck in GNNs is message passing: each node aggregates information from its neighbors repeatedly. Coarse augmentations (like deleting a random edge) disrupt entire neighborhoods, losing too much signal. Fine-grained augmentations, like tweaking individual features, miss the core computational unit: the message itself, the information flowing between neighbors. You need an augmentation that smooths noisy messages and sharpens distinctive ones without destroying the graph structure.
521.ap: This work augments at the message level. For each message flowing between neighbors, it applies a contextual perturbation based on the local neighborhood: if a message is unusual compared to its neighbors, the method sharpens it (amplifies it); if it's generic or noisy, it smooths it. This is done per edge, per layer, per forward pass—fine-grained and adaptive to local context.
521.ww: Messages are the true atomic units of GNN computation. By augmenting at this level, you hit the regularization sweet spot: disrupting enough to prevent memorization, but respecting enough structure to preserve learning signal. Context-aware perturbation (smoothing or sharpening based on neighborhood) is more principled than random deletion because it respects the intrinsic geometry of the graph.
521.po: GNNs trained with MessageShift overfit less and generalize better across diverse graph benchmarks and architectures. It's a general technique applicable to any GNN backbone, and consistently outperforms coarse augmentations.

522.bp: User behavior online is multifaceted: people examine products (looking without commitment), favorite them (expressing interest), and eventually purchase. Recommendations typically predict only one behavior—purchase. But optimizing for long-term satisfaction means predicting all of them: examining and favoring matter for retention and revenue, not just immediate sales.
522.wh: Multi-behavior recommendation means predicting several outcomes simultaneously for the same sequence of actions. The challenge is extracting shared knowledge (user taste is consistent across behaviors) while respecting unique patterns (examining behavior is different from purchasing behavior). Most models apply the same preference learning to all behaviors, which conflates distinct signals. You need both cross-behavior synergy and behavior-specific adaptation.
522.ap: The method learns preferences in three ways in parallel. One module learns cross-behavior patterns (if someone examines many spy thrillers, they'll favorite spy thrillers too). Another learns what information is relevant to each specific behavior (examining might depend more on novelty, purchase on price). A third uses a learned gating mechanism to combine these insights adaptively: for predicting purchase, emphasize certain cues; for predicting examine, emphasize others. A fourth module captures complex sequential patterns specific to each behavior.
522.ww: Multitask learning works by sharing low-level patterns while allowing high-level specialization. Cross-behavior learning captures correlations: if tastes align across behaviors, you get free signal. Behavior-specific modules let each behavior have its own 'interpretation' of what matters. The gating mechanism is crucial: rather than hard-coding which information belongs to which behavior, the model learns this flexibly, adapting based on actual data.
522.po: The system predicts all behaviors accurately, improving long-term user retention and satisfaction. By capturing synergies, it makes better use of sparse data than methods predicting only purchase.

523.bp: Dengue fever spreads through mosquitoes in cities like Singapore; controlling it requires knowing where outbreaks will hit next so resources can be deployed early. Public health agencies have case data (where infections are reported) but lack real-time data on mosquito populations or detailed movement patterns.
523.wh: Standard epidemic models treat cases as independent events, but dengue spreads geographically: infected areas create hotspots that influence neighboring regions. Mosquito movement is localized, but humans travel widely. Existing models miss the long-distance transmission pathways driven by human mobility. Without knowing the actual transmission network structure—who travels between regions—you can't make good predictions.
523.ap: This method infers the hidden transmission network directly from case patterns using gradient descent, the same optimization technique used to train neural networks. It models each region's hotspot status as influenced by case dynamics in other regions, with connection strengths learned from data. The inferred network must explain four weeks of historical hotspot patterns and remain stable when refit on slightly different weeks, ensuring robustness.
523.ww: Transmission networks are latent—you don't observe them directly. But if you posit a network structure and predict what should happen, then compare to actual observed hotspots, you can tune the network to match reality. Requiring the network to be stable across time windows (not radically different if fit on weeks 1-4 vs. weeks 2-5) prevents overfitting to flukes. The learned network ends up reflecting real commuting patterns, providing an interpretable explanation.
523.po: With just four weeks of case history, the model predicts hotspot status in the next week at 79% accuracy (F-score). The learned network aligns with known commuting flows, validating the approach. Even during COVID lockdowns when mobility was disrupted, the model adapted because it learns network structure from data, not fixed assumptions.

524.bp: Documents in regulated industries—insurance contracts, bank statements, medical records—contain sensitive domain-specific knowledge that changes constantly. Extracting structured information (name, address, dates, amounts) from scanned documents is essential for automation, but models trained on public data hallucinate: they generate plausible-sounding answers that aren't in the document.
524.wh: Large multimodal models (systems that read both text and images) can 'understand' anything but hallucinate answers not present in the source. Specialized discriminative models are more reliable but require expensive manual labeling per new domain. Regulated domains forbid sending documents to cloud APIs, so you need to work locally. The real bottleneck is generating enough training data to adapt models without human annotation.
524.ap: This framework auto-generates training data: an agent system processes raw document collections, generates plausible question-answer pairs using a multimodal large language model, verifies them against the source document to filter hallucinations, and distills the results into a lightweight retriever. During inference, the retriever extracts relevant evidence from documents, and the large model generates responses grounded in that evidence, iterating if needed.
524.ww: Synthetic data works when verification is possible. Here, verification is free: check whether the generated QA pair is actually supported by the document. This filters hallucinations at training time. The lightweight retriever is local and fast, so it runs on-device for privacy. The retrieval-grounded loop at inference time prevents hallucination because the model must justify answers with evidence from the retrieved document.
524.po: The system reduces hallucination and improves domain grounding compared to using large models alone, while maintaining privacy (documents never leave the organization). It enables rapid adaptation to new document types without manual annotation, reducing time-to-deployment from weeks to days. Code is released as a Python package for easy integration.
